summary: This Wikipedia article describes social facilitation, the phenomenon in which the presence of others improves individual task performance, especially on simple or well-practiced tasks, while impairing performance on complex or unfamiliar ones. It traces the concept from Triplett's early cycling and competition studies and Floyd Allport's 1924 coinage through Zajonc's drive theory and later activation, evaluation, and attention approaches. The article is flagged as written in an essay style rather than encyclopedic style.
one_line: Overview of social facilitation, the effect of others' presence improving simple-task performance and hindering complex-task performance, with its major theories.
key_facts: Social facilitation is defined in the article as a social phenomenon in which being in the presence of others improves individual task performance.
Norman Triplett first observed social facilitation in cyclists, who rode at faster speeds when competing against other cyclists than when cycling alone.
Meumann (1904) found that during exercise individuals could lift heavier weights when being watched than when not being watched.
Robert Zajonc (1965) theorized that task complexity could influence whether social facilitation occurs.

Zajonc's generalized drive hypothesis held that the presence of others serves as a source of arousal that improves performance on well-learned tasks and impairs performance on complex or not well-learned tasks.
In 1924, Floyd Allport coined the term social facilitation.

Hazel Markus of the University of Michigan found that both audience and incidental audience conditions enhanced performance on the well-learned aspects of dressing and undressing with familiar clothing and hindered performance on unfamiliar clothing.

A 2010 study found that donation rates increased with the presence of observers, and neuroimaging showed observers significantly affected activation in the ventral striatum before the choice to donate.
Henchy and Glass proposed the evaluation approach in 1968 through their evaluation apprehension hypothesis, which holds that fear of being evaluated by an audience drives arousal.
Nickolas Cottrell developed Evaluation Apprehension Theory in 1972.
Robert Baron proposed distraction-conflict theory, in which distractions can produce social facilitation on simple tasks but impair performance on complex tasks.
The overload hypothesis holds that distracters lead to cognitive overload rather than increased arousal, improving simple-task performance and impairing complex-task performance.

The capacity model holds that the presence of others does not hinder automatic information processing but impedes controlled information processing because short-term memory is needed for both focusing and monitoring the audience.
Raefeli's 2002 meta-analysis concluded that social facilitation effects are surprisingly unrelated to the performer's evaluation apprehension.
